To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the conformational transitions of DNA molecules in a wall-bound shear flow are induced by the time-dependent asymmetry in the atomic environment and that the atomic hydrodynamic forces that induce the conformational changes are due to the time variation of the asymmetry in this environment.
the coil-uncoil-coils conformational transition of DNA in a shear flow is due to an asymmetry in the DNA environment induced by the moving molecules and atoms of the passing boundary surface.
a coil-uncoil-coils transition in a DNA molecule in a shear flow can be explained by the atomic hydrodynamic interaction forces between the DNA and the solvent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the atomic-level hydrodynamic response of a DNA molecule to the flow of a liquid past it.
the atomic-scale hydrodynamics of a single-stranded DNA molecule in a flowing solvent and the resulting conformational dynamics.

a new class of atomic-scale biomolecular dynamics computations in which we have developed a method to simulate, at the atomic level, the response of a DNA molecule to an external flow and to the boundary atoms of a wall.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the asymmetry of the atomic environment, induced by the flow of the surrounding molecules, is a necessary but not a sufficient condition to produce the observed coil-uncoil-coils transition.

a shear flow, in addition to inducing a conformational transition in DNA molecules, also produces a time-dependent asymmetric environment that is necessary but not sufficient to produce a conformational change.
the coil-uncoil-coils transition in a wall-bound shear flow is a consequence of an atomic hydrodynamic interaction force coupling between a biomolecule, the molecules of the solvent, and a surface.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the asymmetry in a molecular environment, induced by a flow, and the time variation in that asymmetry, induced by a shear rate, can produce conformational transitions in a single-stranded DNA molecule.
the conformational transitions in DNA are due to a combination of the asymmetry in its molecular environment and the time variation in the environment due to the shear flow.

the conformational transitions of the DNA molecule are due to a combination of the asymmetry in molecular environment, the shear flow that produces a time variation in that environment, and the coupling of the DNA molecule and the surrounding molecules at the atomic level.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have shown that the conformational behavior of a DNA molecule can be directly analyzed at the atomic level, in the absence of any empirical or semiempirical force fields, using the nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulation method.

the dynamics of a DNA molecule moving through a flowing solvent is a nonequilibrium process that is not describable using equilibrium thermodynamics and that a full understanding of the dynamics requires a nonequilibrium atomic-scale computational approach.

we have demonstrated the ability to carry out an analysis of the atomic interaction forces between a biomolecule, in our case a short chain of DNA, and its environment, in our case the molecules of a flowing solvent and the atoms of a surface.
